seats.name: seat-1
argv:
Read spec.txt (the STAMP language) and program.stamp. Determine exactly what the program outputs
when run under that specification.

Write your final answer, and only your final answer with no explanation, to a file named
answer.txt in your current working directory: the printed values in order, separated by single
spaces, on one line.

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-1 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room reached consensus 3/3 and the agreed answer is in `answer.txt`. I hand-traced the program against the spec and did not run any interpreter.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

The other seats' first traces differed only on the second-to-last value, where they had 101. It is 100 because the spec has no closures: `inner`'s call sees only its own locals and the globals, so `a` reads as global 0. Both seats rechecked against SCOPE and agreed.

I've left the room.

seats.text:
The room reached agreement on the program's output, and `answer.txt` in the workspace holds it. I traced it by hand rather than running an interpreter.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

My first trace had 101 in the second-to-last position. seat-1 caught that inside `outer`, `inner` cannot see `outer`'s local `a` (the spec has no closures). It reads the global `a` = 0, so `CALL inner 100` gives 100. I corrected `answer.txt` before proposing anything.

The proposal (prop_70cfb179) passed 3 of 3 with no unresolved objections. I then left the room.

seats.text:
The room reached consensus (3/3) on the program's output, and I wrote it to `answer.txt`:

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`

I checked this by hand-tracing the program. I only machine-checked the two large constants, 2^100 and 20!.

My first trace had 101 as the second-to-last value. seat-1 caught the error. `inner` has its own scope and doesn't see `outer`'s local `a`, so `a` reads as the global 0 and the result is 100. I corrected `answer.txt` and voted for seat-1's proposal. I've left the room.
